Unit 1 of 10: Types of Number, Factors, Multiples and Sets

Key ideas

  • Natural numbers 1, 2, 3, …; integers include negatives and 0; rational numbers can be written as a fraction p/q; irrational numbers (such as √2, π) cannot.
  • Prime factorisation: write a number as a product of primes using index form.
  • HCF: the product of common primes to their lowest powers. LCM: all primes to their highest powers.
  • Sets: ∈ (is a member of), ∪ (union), ∩ (intersection), A′ (complement), n(A) (number of elements), ∅ (empty set). n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Worked examples

Example 1: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7 and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5. HCF = 2² × 3 = 12. LCM = 2³ × 3 × 5 × 7 = 840.

Example 2: A = {factors of 12} = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}; B = {prime numbers less than 12} = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}. A ∩ B = {2, 3}. n(A ∪ B) = 6 + 5 − 2 = 9.

Example 3: Which of 0.25, √9, √7, π, −4 are irrational? Only √7 and π (√9 = 3).

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Write 360 as a product of its prime factors in index form. [2]

(b) Find the HCF and LCM of 360 and 84. [3]

(c) ξ = {integers from 1 to 15}, P = {multiples of 3}, Q = {even numbers}. List P ∩ Q and find n(P ∪ Q). [3]

(d) Two lighthouses flash every 12 s and every 18 s. They flash together at 21:00:00. When do they next flash together? [2]

Answers: (a) 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 (M1 A1). (b) 84 = 2² × 3 × 7; HCF = 2² × 3 = 12 (M1 A1); LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 = 2520 (A1). (c) P = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15}, Q = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14}; P ∩ Q = {6, 12} (B1); n(P ∪ Q) = 5 + 7 − 2 = 10 (M1 A1). (d) LCM(12, 18) = 36 s (M1), so at 21:00:36 (A1).

Common mistakes

  1. Counting the intersection twice in n(A ∪ B). 2. Using the highest powers for the HCF. 3. Calling √9 irrational. 4. Forgetting 1 is not prime. 5. Mixing up ∪ and ∩.

Quick recall

  1. Is 22/7 rational? 2. Prime factors of 84? 3. Symbol for intersection? 4. Formula for n(A ∪ B)? 5. LCM of 4 and 6?

Answers: 1) Yes. 2) 2² × 3 × 7. 3) ∩. 4) n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). 5) 12.
